newsitem.title: USA: Platinum closes higher, grains mixed on USDA.
newsitem.headline: Platinum closes higher, grains mixed on USDA.

text.p: Precious metals prices ended firm on Friday as doubts about fresh Russian supplies buoyed the platinum group.
Platinum for October delivery at the New York Mercantile Exchange jumped $14.00 to end at $395.70 an ounce, with September palladium closing up $4.60 at $153.00 an ounce.

The physical platinum and palladium market remained tight, although Japanese trade houses reported this week that some Russian palladium had finally arrived in Japan. Platinum was not due to arrive until next week.

Platinum group exports from Russia had been suspended since last December. Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and 20 percent of its platinum. The metals play key roles in electronics and auto manufacturing.
This week's shipments to Japan were under long-term deals just negotiated with the trade houses.
But news reports on Friday also suggested that the Russians had decided not to offer more platinum in the spot or cash market due to limited supplies of the metal in Russia.

"Platinum and palladium may also have already anticipated the Russian return to the market, and short-covering may push prices higher next week also," said Refco metals analyst Jim Steel of Friday's bounce in prices.
The firmness in platinum aided gold, and the contract for August delivery at COMEX ended up $1.40 at $322.20 an ounce. September silver ended down 2.3 cents at $4.360 an ounce.

"Silver saw fund selling in Europe overnight, but gold ended near the top of the week's range, helped by some physical buying around $315 earlier in the week and some fund short-covering," Steel said.
Gold prices on Wednesday hit a 12-year low of $315.75 in London after the Reserve Bank of Australia sold 167 metric tons of gold, or two-thirds of its reserves.
On Friday, a 0.1 percent fall in the U.S. June producer price index, the sixth consecutive monthly drop in the inflation gauge, further cut gold's appeal as an inflation hedge for investors.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain prices closed mixed with Midwest weather and monthly Agriculture Department crop estimates providing the main impetus for trading.

Wheat for July delivery closed up 1/2 cent a bushel at $3.22 after the department estimated total wheat production this year at 2.43 billion bushels, slightly below most analysts' estimates. Sharp cuts in spring and durum wheat offset a rise in winter wheat output.
The government cut its estimate for corn production to 9.7 billion bushels, down 140 million from last month. July corn closed up 3-3/4 cents a bushel at $2.51-1/2.
"Next week's rain event or non-rain event will do more to flat prices than any of these numbers," said John Zanutto, vice president for Merrill Lynch Futures.
Corn in the Midwest is entering its pollination stage, a crucial period when heat and moisture play a major role in forming ears on the corn plants and shaping grain yields.

Soybean prices closed near the highest levels of the day with weather forecasts issued after the noon hour suggesting that the heaviest rains next week would fall to the north of a few dry pockets in central Illinois and eastern Iowa.
July soybeans closed up 6-1/2 cents a bushel at $7.85-1/2, while contracts for delivery after the harvest closed lower.

The government said remaining stocks of soybeans in the United States will be tight before the fall harvest, but it also raised its estimate for this year's soybean crop to 2.690 billion bushels, a record.
Oil prices ended higher in quiet trade as crude traders waited for news on the restart of limited Iraqi oil sales, and gasoline trading took center stage on the heels of action in spot markets.
Crude oil futures for August delivery settled 11 cents higher at $19.33 a barrel.
"We're waiting to see what happens on Sunday," said Marcy Forsyth, a trader at Refco in New York.

The United Nations' humanitarian coordinator in Iraq is scheduled to meet Sunday in Baghdad with Iraqi officials and may receive a completed plan on how Iraq plans to distribute aid received through proceeds from the limited oil sales.

A distribution plan acceptable to the U.N. Secretary-General is key to restarting Iraq's crude exports, which are expected to resume at a rate of at least 730,000 barrels per day. Iraq is allowed limited sales to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian aid.
August gasoline closed up 0.66 cent a gallon at 59.26 cents and August heating oil up 0.24 cent a gallon at 52.35 cents.
